intro:
Escape from Capua — 73 BC

Spartacus, the escape has begun. The gladiatorial school is behind you, but the roads ahead still belong to Rome. Get your people away before the local guards can gather a force large enough to surround them.

Reach an escape hex and evacuate at least one unit. The immediate purpose is survival: a band that reaches the country around Vesuvius can find shelter and grow; one trapped outside the school has no future.

Ancient accounts describe a small group breaking out of the school of Lentulus Batiatus with improvised weapons. The exact size of the band and the details of Spartacus's earlier life are uncertain. This map stages the escape, rather than reproducing a documented route.

intro:
Gathering the fugitives — 73 BC

You are free of Capua, but freedom without food or weapons will not last. The surrounding estates and roads can supply the band, and other enslaved people are looking for a chance to join it.

Capture the four marked objectives. Keep enough fighters together to protect the growing force while detachments secure supplies. Rome has not yet committed its strongest armies, but local resistance can still destroy small groups caught alone.

Spartacus, Crixus and Oenomaus emerged as leaders of the rising. Your task is to turn fugitives into a force capable of surviving the response that must follow.

intro:
Vesuvius — 73 BC

Glaber's Roman force has moved against the rebels around Vesuvius. He expects the mountain and its limited approaches to hold you in place until hunger does his work.

Break the encirclement and seize the two marked Roman positions. Keep the band concentrated until a route is open, then strike where the besiegers cannot support one another. Remaining behind your own defences only gives Rome time to bring up more men.

The ancient tradition describes an unexpected descent from the mountain and an attack on the Roman camp. This scenario gives you the same problem: escape a seemingly secure cordon by taking the initiative.

intro:
Nola — 73 BC

The band has grown, and the towns of Campania contain both the supplies it needs and the people who may join it. Nola is the next objective.

Capture the city before the Roman response catches up with you. Use the approach routes to gather the force for one coordinated assault; scattered attacks give the garrison time to defeat the leading groups separately.

The scenario imagines help from enslaved people inside the town. Treat that as part of its setting, not a guarantee that the gates will open through a scripted event. You must take the marked Nola objective with the troops on the map.

intro:
Acerrae: Furius — 73 BC

Varinius has sent detachments ahead of his main force. Furius is within reach, and defeating him before the Roman columns unite offers the rebels a chance to keep the initiative.

Take the marked enemy position and break the force guarding it. Concentrate the attack and keep a reserve against troops approaching from the surrounding roads. A victory here is valuable because it leaves one fewer Roman detachment to face in the next battle.

Ancient accounts name Furius among Varinius's defeated subordinates. The campaign's choice of Acerrae as the battlefield is a reconstruction, not an established location.

intro:
The camp of Cossinius — 73 BC

Cossinius commands another part of Varinius's force. His camp is exposed before the main Roman army can come to its support; strike while the opportunity lasts.

Capture the marked positions and deny the defenders room to regroup. Send enough men to secure the approaches while the main body attacks, rather than allowing the whole band to become absorbed in one corner of the camp.

The ancient account associates Cossinius with a place called Salinae. Its location is uncertain; this scenario uses the Herculaneum area as its setting. The operational problem is to defeat a separated Roman force before it can join the others.

intro:
Escape from Varinius — 73 BC

Varinius has brought up his main army. The camp that sheltered the band is becoming a trap, and a prolonged siege would consume the supplies before it broke the Romans.

Open a route through the cordon and evacuate nine units through the escape hexes. Keep a rearguard between the withdrawing columns and the Roman main body; the strongest fighters are needed to cover the movement, not to win an unnecessary battle for the old camp.

The map also offers a holding result for retaining an objective at the turn limit. The narrative task is to save the band so it can continue the revolt. Do not leave the slowest units to make the last part of the journey alone.

intro:
Nuceria — 73 BC

The escape has kept the army together, but Varinius is still following. Nuceria lies on the route ahead, offering supplies and a place to gather more followers before the pursuit closes in again.

Capture the marked Nuceria positions and the remaining objective. Keep a force watching the approaches behind you while the main body clears the town. An army crowded into captured streets can be as vulnerable as one caught in a camp.

This stage represents the rebels' movement through Campania. The point is to keep the rising supplied and mobile while Rome is still struggling to concentrate against it.

intro:
Picentia: turn on Varinius — 73 BC

Varinius continues the pursuit. As long as his army remains intact, every halt for food or recruits becomes another chance for Rome to surround you.

Turn against the pursuit and capture the three marked positions. Bring the fighters together for the attack, then prevent the Roman detachments from retreating into a single defensible group. Breaking this army will give the revolt room to move beyond its first refuge.

The ancient sources describe Varinius's defeat but do not securely locate this battlefield. Picentia is the campaign author's chosen setting.

intro:
Spartacus or Crixus — 72 BC

The revolt has become large enough to contain more than one purpose. Some followers want a way out of Italy; others intend to continue the war against Rome on Italian ground.

Choose the campaign route of Spartacus or Crixus using the selection map. The following battles will place you with the chosen group. This is a decision about whose march to follow, not an ordinary battle for territory.

Ancient accounts record the separation of Crixus's force, but do not establish a single certain explanation for it. The campaign turns that separation into a choice for the player.

intro:
Mons Garganus: Crixus — 72 BC

Rome is sending consular forces against the rising. Crixus's group faces the troops associated in this scenario with Arrius, ahead of Gellius's main force.

Attack the Roman camp and capture the marked positions before the enemy can concentrate. Keep the group together after the first success; possession of a camp is not protection against another army approaching it.

This is the Crixus route: do not deploy Spartacus. Historically Crixus's force was defeated near Mount Garganus. A victory here opens the campaign's fictional continuation of his command.

intro:
Gellius: Crixus's continuation — 72 BC

Alternate-history branch: Crixus has survived the encounter at Mons Garganus and defeated Arrius. Gellius is bringing a larger Roman force to restore the situation.

Take the marked positions, including Siponto and Herdonia, and prevent the Roman columns from enclosing your army. You will need more than the momentum of the last victory: draw the defenders apart, then concentrate against the sector that opens a route through them.

Remain with the Crixus force and do not deploy Spartacus. This battle imagines a campaign Crixus did not live to conduct.

intro:
Lentulus blocks the road — 72 BC

Spartacus, a consular army under Lentulus stands across the march north. Another Roman force is approaching from behind. Waiting allows them to close the trap together.

Break the force in front of you and capture the marked objectives, including Cliternia. Keep the main body moving through the breach while a rearguard watches the pursuit. The purpose is a road north for the army, not a long occupation of every Roman camp.

This is the Spartacus route: do not deploy Crixus. The campaign represents the rebel victories over the separated consular forces before they could bring their full strength to bear.

intro:
Turn against Gellius — 72 BC

Lentulus has been driven back, but the pursuit from the south still threatens your rear. News of Crixus's defeat has reached the army, and Gellius's force now stands in the way of a secure march.

Turn against the pursuers, take the marked positions and keep Cliternia under control. Strike with the main body before the Romans can join the troops already beaten on the northern road.

Do not deploy Crixus on this route. Ancient accounts link Spartacus's subsequent fighting with commemoration of the fallen rebel leader; the battle itself still has to be won by keeping the surviving army together.

intro:
Cisalpine Gaul — 72 BC

The road north has brought the rebels into Cisalpine Gaul. Roman forces under Cassius stand between the army and the approaches to the Alps.

Take Mutina, Regium Lepidum and the remaining marked objective. Keep the march concentrated until the Roman line is broken; scattered columns cannot force a route through a formed army.

The prospect of leaving Italy gives this battle its urgency. Ancient accounts describe a rebel victory over Cassius, followed by a return south. They do not let us recover with certainty every reason for that change of direction.

intro:
Firmum Picenum — 72 BC

The army is marching south again, and Roman forces are gathering across its route. They have been beaten before, but each delay gives them another chance to unite.

Capture Firmum Picenum, Ancona, Auximum and the other marked position. Keep the roads between the objectives open so the army can move as one body rather than a string of isolated detachments.

This scenario reconstructs the renewed fighting in central Italy. Its precise battlefield and deployment are campaign choices. Rome remains the power behind the pursuing armies; taking these towns is a means to sustain the revolt, not an assault on the capital itself.

intro:
Break Crassus's cordon — 71 BC

Crassus has trapped the rebels in southern Italy behind a line of fortifications. The plan to cross to Sicily with Cilician pirates has failed, and supplies are running down.

Force a passage through the cordon and evacuate ten units. Choose a sector where you can concentrate, hold the breach against counterattack and bring the slower troops through before committing the rearguard.

Ancient accounts describe the pirates taking payment without providing the promised passage. There is no fleet coming to rescue the army in these orders: the route back into Italy must be opened on land.

intro:
Relieve the separated camp — 71 BC

The group led by Castus and Gannicus has separated from Spartacus. Crassus is moving against it, seeking to destroy one part of the rising before the others can intervene.

March to support the threatened force and secure the marked positions around Metapontum, Heraclea and Grumentum. At the turn limit, holding three, two or one objectives earns a Brilliant Victory, Victory or Tactical Victory respectively.

The rescue gives the battle its urgency: draw the Romans away from the isolated group without allowing your own leading troops to be surrounded. This is a reconstruction of the fighting between separated rebel forces and Crassus's increasingly organised army.

intro:
The final battle — 71 BC

Crassus's army blocks the route ahead. The revolt has lost men through repeated separations and battles, and another Roman army under Pompey is returning to Italy. There is less and less room in which to escape.

Take Paestum and the other marked objectives, break the Roman position and keep the army concentrated for the decisive attack. Do not spend its strength on disconnected assaults that leave the main line untouched.

The campaign places its final battle near Paestum. The exact location of Spartacus's last stand is disputed, and the ancient sources do not securely identify his body. Your result here is the campaign's ending, not a claim to settle those uncertainties.
